content: Argentina anserina, commonly referred to as Silverweed, is a perennial flowering plant belonging to the Rosaceae family. It is native to the temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere and is frequently found along riverbanks and in grassy environments such as meadows and roadsides. Previously classified under the genus Potentilla, it has been reclassified into the genus Argentina. Silverweed is a low-growing herbaceous plant characterized by creeping red stolons that can extend up to 80 cm in length. Its leaves measure 10–20 cm in length and are evenly pinnate, with crenate leaflets that are 2–5 cm long and 1–2 cm wide. These leaflets are covered in silky white hairs, particularly on their undersides, which also extend to the stems and stolons. This silvery appearance of the leaves is the origin of the plant's common name. The flowers are approximately 5 cm in diameter and typically have five yellow petals, though occasionally up to seven. The fruit is a cluster of dry achenes. Distinguishing Argentina anserina from Argentina egedii, the only other species in the genus, can be challenging. The two species differ primarily in the characteristics of their hairs. Some botanists consider Argentina egedii to be a subspecies of Argentina anserina. Silverweed is most commonly found in sandy or gravelly soils, where it spreads rapidly through its prolific rooting stolons. Unlike Argentina egedii, which is a salt-tolerant coastal saltmarsh plant, Silverweed is typically found in inland habitats. Cultivation and Uses The underground roots of Silverweed have been used to prepare herbal tea, which is believed to aid in childbirth and act as an antispasmodic for diarrhea. Historically, the plant was placed in shoes to absorb sweat. According to Howard (1987), it was once used as a treatment for epilepsy and was thought to ward off witches and evil spirits. Silverweed has also been cultivated as a food crop for its edible roots. However, the wild forms of the plant are generally impractical for this purpose due to their small size and the difficulty of cleaning them. Additionally, Silverweed can become an invasive weed in gardens. Etymology and Folklore The pre-Linnaean name anserina translates to of the goose (from the Latin Anser), possibly because the plant was used to feed geese or because its leaves resemble the footprints of geese. Silverweed has a rich folklore associated with it. In French, it is commonly called richette, a name that reflects its association with both silver and gold.
